## Binomial properties

Use `choose` or `factorial` to count the number of ways to have x successes in n total trials.

```{r}
n <- 3
x <- 2

choose(n, x)

factorial(n) / (factorial(x) * factorial(n - x))
```


We can use `dbinom` to calculate a specific binomial probability, or multiple probabilities.

```{r}
dbinom(x = 2, size = 3, prob = 0.6)

dbinom(0:3, 3, 0.6)
```


Recall the powerplant example, where we calculated the distribution of the number of girl births assuming a null of 50/50 boy or girl.

```{r}
birth_null_proportions <- tibble(
  prop_girls = replicate(10000,
                         mean(sample(0:1, size = 300,
                                     replace = T, prob = c(0.5, 0.5))))
)

# Two-sided pvalue
mean(birth_null_proportions$prop_girls >= 0.52) +
  mean(birth_null_proportions$prop_girls <= 0.48)
```

How would we calculate this with an exact binomial probability?  The null distribution can be described as $Binom(300, 0.5)$.  The results are very similar.

```{r}
# Two-sided pvalue, from binomial distribution
sum(dbinom(156:300, 300, 0.5)) +
  sum(dbinom(0:144, 300, 0.5))
```

EX 9.2 Binomial test example

A psychic claims to be able to guess the suit of a card without knowing. In 200 card draws, they get 57 correct.  Perform a test of the null hypothesis $H_0: p = 0.25$ at the 1% level.

First, use the simulation of the null distribution:

```{r}
# Simulation of null distribution of number of correct cards
card_null_proportions <- tibble(
  prop_correct = replicate(10000,
                         mean(sample(0:1, size = 200,
                                     replace = T, prob = c(0.75, 0.25))))
)
```

Next, find a p-value without simulation, with the binomial distribution.  The results should be very similar.


## Normal distribution

`pnorm` finds a lower-tail normal probability (area under the curve).

```{r}
# P(N(0, 1) <= 0.5)
pnorm(0.5, 0, 1)
```

For the area above, use a negative or `lower.tail = F`.

```{r}
# P(N(0, 1) >= 0.5)
1 - pnorm(0.5, 0, 1)
pnorm(0.5, 0, 1, lower.tail = F)
```

Find a specific percentile with `qnorm`.

```{r}
# 30th percentile of N(0, 1)
qnorm(0.3, 0, 1)
```

`pnorm` and `qnorm` are inverses!

```{r}
qnorm(0.3, 0, 1)

pnorm(-0.5244005)
```

## Central Limit Theorem

Recall the D&D example, where we looked at the distribution of ability scores.  For a single score, the distribution goes from 3-18 and is asymmetric.

```{r}
generate_score <- function() {
  rolls <- sample(1:6, 4, replace = TRUE)   # Roll dice
  keep <- sort(rolls)[2:4]       # Keep highest 3 rolls
  sum(keep)
}

strength_values <- tibble(
  run = 1:10000,
  values = replicate(10000, generate_score())
)

ggplot(strength_values, aes(x = values)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 2.5,
                 fill = "goldenrod2", color = "black")
```

When we looked at the average of six scores, the resulting distribution was more closely concentrated around 12.2.

```{r}
all_character_scores <- function(){
  setNames(replicate(n = 6, generate_score()),
           c("STR", "DEX", "CON", "INT", "WIS", "CHA"))
}

average_scores <- tibble(
  run = 1:10000,
  values = replicate(10000, mean(all_character_scores())) 
)

ggplot(average_scores, aes(x = values)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "dodgerblue", color = "black")
```

In general, when we draw a sample from a population, the sample mean has an approximately normal sampling distribution.  This approximation is better when:
- The original population is more symmetric/normal
- n is large

Consider a skewed population like "miles per gallon".

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "goldenrod2", color = "black", bins = 20)
```

Let's look at the sample mean of 5 draws, and then 20 draws.

```{r}
new_data <- function(data, n) {
  sample_n(data, size = n, replace = TRUE)
}
```

When n = 5, the asymmetry is still present.

```{r}
average_mpg_5 <- tibble(
  run = 1:10000,
  xbars = replicate(10000,
                    mean(new_data(mtcars, 5)$mpg) ) 
)

ggplot(average_mpg_5, aes(x = xbars)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "dodgerblue", color = "black")
```

When n = 20, the sampling distribution looks normal (and also has less spread!)

```{r}
average_mpg_20 <- tibble(
  run = 1:10000,
  xbars = replicate(10000,
                    mean(new_data(mtcars, 20)$mpg) ) 
)

ggplot(average_mpg_20, aes(x = xbars)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "dodgerblue", color = "black")
```

Usually, n = 30 is "good enough" to apply the CLT in most cases.
